keyVerseText: And he took it down, and wrapped it in linen, and laid it in a sepulchre that was hewn in stone, wherein never man before was laid.
rootMeaning: The word οὐδέπω (oudépō) derives from the combination of οὐδέ (oude), meaning 'not even' or 'neither,' and the particle πω (pō), which conveys the sense of 'yet' or 'still.' This etymology highlights a nuanced negation that emphasizes something has not occurred up to the present moment but may still occur in the future. Unlike a simple negation, it carries a temporal dimension, implying a situation is ongoing and incomplete.
usageInScripture: Οὐδέπω appears five times in the New Testament, consistently carrying the sense of 'not yet,' 'never before,' or 'as yet not.' Its translations range from 'man' in one context to temporal negations like 'not yet' and 'never,' reflecting its role in expressing that an event or action has not happened previously or at the time of speaking. This consistency shows its function as an adverb marking an unfinished or unprecedented state.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding οὐδέπω enriches our grasp of biblical temporality and God's unfolding plan. It reminds believers that certain divine actions or fulfillments have not yet occurred but are anticipated in God's perfect timing. This word invites patience and trust in God's sovereignty, recognizing that what has 'not yet' happened is part of His redemptive narrative. It also underscores the uniqueness of Christ's work, often marking moments that have never occurred before, highlighting the newness brought through Him.
keyVerseReflection: In Luke 23:53, the phrase 'wherein never man before was laid' uses οὐδέπω to emphasize the unprecedented nature of the tomb in which Jesus was placed. This word accentuates that no one had ever been laid there previously, underscoring the singularity of Christ's burial. It invites reflection on how Jesus' death and resurrection inaugurate a new reality, one that had not existed before and points to the fulfillment of God's redemptive plan.
